summary: Lunar Mission Planner is an open-source web app that lets mission planners, educators and the public judge a lunar landing site and date in seconds. Spin a 3D Moon globe, pick one of 25 sourced sites (Apollo, CLPS, Artemis III regions, other nations) or type any coordinates, and get three plain-language answers: Power, Talk to Earth, and Landing (slope). A Python pipeline converts NASA SPICE ephemeris and LRO LOLA terrain (120 m near the south pole) into compact files; the browser then traces the real terrain skyline, with no atmosphere, and finds when the Sun and Earth clear it for any date from 2026 to 2035. A timeline with time-lapse, first-person surface view, sunset and Earthset countdowns, a “Move a little” sensitivity check, and side-by-side comparison of up to four sites or dates address the challenge directly, including schedule slips. Results match JPL Horizons to about 0.00005° and pass 190 automated tests. It matters because moving a few hundred metres, or slipping one launch date, can decide whether a south-pole lander has power and a link to Earth.
details:
Overview

Lunar Mission Planner is a web app for choosing a lunar landing site and date. It shows when a site has sunlight and Earth in view, and, whether the ground is flat enough to land on. We built it for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge Lunar Landing Site Navigator. A mission that launches late lands under different conditions: the site may be on a steep slope, in low sunlight, or out of line of sight with Earth, so the rover can’t power itself or communicate. The planner lets teams check this before they commit.

What it does and how it works

A Python pipeline runs once to prepare the data. The web app then runs every calculation in the browser, with no backend server.

  • Sun and Earth positions: Taken from NASA JPL SPICE kernels, sampled every 30 minutes and interpolated in the browser, for any date from 2026 to 2035.
  • Terrain horizon: For each point, the engine marches over the terrain in 720 directions, up to 200 km, including the Moon’s curvature. The Sun or Earth counts as “in view” when it clears that horizon.
  • Mission metrics: Over the mission window, it reports the share of time with the Sun up, Earth in view, and both. It also reports the longest dark stretches and the next five viable windows. There is a “Count partial Sun” option.
  • Ratings: The Sun, Earth and Landing cards each give a rating badge, a plain-language verdict and a “why” checklist. Landing is “Possible” if the plane-fit slope over a 100 m disc is under 8°.

Features

  1. Interactive 3D Moon Globe: A 3D Moon with a real day/night line, IAU crater names and a lat/lon grid, controllable by mouse or keyboard.
  2. Landing Mission Checkpoints: 25 historic and planned mission sites pinned on the globe, grouped by mission type, each citing its source.
  3. Compare Up to 4 Landing Sites: Side-by-side statistics, line charts and every other value needed to compare sites, with presets like “Equator vs pole” and “Two Artemis III regions.”
  4. Earth Visibility Calendar: Days are marked green when Earth is visible from the chosen site for at least one hour.
  5. Timeline Chart: A 29.5-day strip with separate rows for Sun, Earth and both, which you can scrub through.
  6. Quick Search: Search by mission landing site or type coordinates in several formats to jump to a location and see its statistics.
  7. Mission Length: Set the stay to 6.5 days (based on NASA’s Artemis III surface stay) or 14 days, and see the next five viable windows.
  8. Sun Elevation and Sunlight Duration: The Sun’s elevation and how long it stays up for any point on the Moon.
  9. Earth Visibility: Earth’s elevation and how long it stays above the local horizon, which decides direct communication, for any point.
  10. First-Person Surface View: The sky from the chosen point, with the terrain skyline and the paths of the Sun and Earth.
  11. Play Button: Animates the movement of the Sun and Earth as real astronomical bodies on the globe and the surface view, from 1 hour to 3 days per second.
  12. Move a Little: Samples eight points around the pin (250 m to 1 km) to show how sensitive the results are to small shifts in position.
  13. South Polar Map: A separate 3D polar HD map (84°S to the pole, 120 m) for the region that is hardest for mission planners, where every other feature still works.
  14. Antenna Height: Set the antenna to 2, 5, 10 or 15 m and see how Earth visibility changes.
  15. Landing Slope: Click any point on the polar map to see whether it is possible to land there, using a plane-fit slope over a 100 m disc.
  16. Quick Collaboration: The link holds the full view state, so you can copy it, send it to anyone, and they open exactly what you saw.
  17. Slope, PSR, and Sunlight Overlay: Red zones mark slopes dangerous for landing, permanently shaded regions (PSR) mark where ice or water may exist, and an average-sunlight overlay runs from dark to golden for the best sunlight.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Teams can compare candidate sites in minutes and spot problems early, such as long darkness, poor Earth visibility or unsafe slopes.
  • It supports planning for the south polar region, which is both the hardest for mission planners and of high interest for water ice in permanently shaded areas.
  • After comparing landing sites, you can share the result with anyone as a single link. They open it and see exactly what you shared, and they can send their own findings back the same way. Teams, advisors and students can review, discuss and refine site choices together, with no accounts, installs or file exports.
  • The first-person surface view lets any student or member of the public get a feel for standing on the Moon. They see the real terrain skyline at the chosen site, then play the time-lapse to watch the Sun and Earth move across the sky, dip behind ridges and skim the horizon. It makes clear why the lunar south pole is such a hard place to land and operate.
  • Plain-language verdicts and “Show the science” details make it usable by students, planners and experts alike.
  • The project is open source under Apache-2.0.

Tools, languages and data

  • Web app: React 19, Vite, Zustand, CesiumJS (3D globe), three.js (surface view), Leaflet, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, Web Workers (horizon calculations), TypeScript/JavaScript on Node.js 22
  • Data pipeline: Python 3.11+ with spiceypy, numpy, scipy, rasterio, pyproj, pillow and requests
  • Testing and quality: Vitest (190 tests), oxlint, axe-core accessibility checks
  • Deployment: Vercel
  • Data sources: NASA JPL NAIF SPICE kernels, LOLA 20 m south pole DEM (NASA PGDA), LOLA GDR global terrain (~1.9 km), NASA average-illumination and PSR layers, IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature (USGS), NSSDCA/LROC landing-site positions, LRO WAC imagery via NASA Moon Trek (display only), and JPL Horizons for validation
  • Hardware: No special hardware. It runs in an ordinary web browser, with no server-side compute or GPU server.

How it is creative

  • It turns raw ephemeris and terrain data into a first-person view of the sky from the surface, with the Sun and Earth moving across the terrain skyline.
  • The Play button animates the Sun and Earth like real astronomical bodies on both the globe and the surface view.
  • The “Move a little” check shows how sensitive a site’s results are to small shifts in position.
  • Three short interactive welcome slides explain the Sun’s path, liberation and antenna clearance.
  • After comparing landing sites, any scenario can be shared as a link. Anyone can open it, see exactly what was shared, and share their own view back. This makes site selection a collaborative, back-and-forth conversation instead of screenshots and spreadsheets.
  • Next, we plan a plain-language assistant. A planner could ask for “the best landing site inside Shackleton crater for a 6.5-day stay in March 2029.” The app would answer with pins, timeline and compare view, and explain its reasoning on request, using the existing validated engine.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons within 0.000044°. Horizon results match an independent Python reference within 0.00001°. A benchmark against NASA PGDA agrees within about 0.1 points for Earth visibility and 1.3 points for sunlight.
  • Accessibility: Axe-core WCAG 2.1 A/AA checks, focus rings, keyboard controls and a mobile layout down to 360 px.
  • Transparency about limits: The 120 m and 240 m grids miss features smaller than a few hundred metres. Landing ratings use slope only and ignore boulders and roughness. Global terrain is coarse and has no landing rating. Communication relays are not modeled. The 8-day Sun level and 8° slope cutoff are our own judgements, not NASA figures.
    • Plain-language mission assistant: A planner asks, "Best landing site inside Shackleton crater for a 6.5-day stay in March 2029?" The app answers with pins, the best timeline window and a compare view. It explains each decision on request, using our validated engine rather than guessing.
    • Solar power generation estimation: Estimate how much electricity a lander or rover could generate at a specific site, using the Sun and shadow data the app already computes.
    • Season heatmap: A year-at-a-glance view that shows the best dates for sunlight and Earth visibility at a site.
    • Site report export: A one-click downloadable summary of a site's ratings, charts and assumptions for proposals and reviews.
    • Live moving shadows: Terrain shadows that sweep across the surface as time plays.
    • Safer landing and communication checks: Add boulder and roughness hazards, higher-resolution terrain beyond the polar region, and communication-relay modeling.
